findings.title: Unknown/unrecognized severity silently downgraded P1→P3 and normalization dropped
findings.whyItBreaks: Base code canonicalized raw.severity via String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() and defaulted unparseable/missing severity to "P1" (fail-cautious). Head removes the normalization and changes the fallback to "P3". Concretely: "p1".trim().toUpperCase()="P1" (base: P1) vs "p1" ∉ SEVERITIES (head: P3); undefined/"" (base: P1) vs (head: P3); " P0 " (base: P0) vs (head: P3). A finding the reviewer meant to be P0/P1 is now labeled low-risk P3, and the exact fallback branch cannot be distinguished from an explicitly-set P3 — the failure signal is discarded. The function's name promises normalization; the body no longer normalizes the value.

findings.title: Severity normalization dropped; invalid severity defaults to P3
findings.whyItBreaks: Old code normalized with String(raw.severity ?? "").trim().toUpperCase() and fell back to "P1"; new code exact-matches raw.severity against uppercase SEVERITIES with no trim/case handling, and falls back to "P3". An LLM-emitted severity of "p1", " P2 ", or "P0\n" previously matched and was returned as-is; it now falls through to "P3" (lowest), and a missing severity now also reports P3 instead of P1. A high-severity finding is reported as low-priority, masking real defects to the review consumer.

findings.title: Severity fallback and normalization regressed (P1→P3, no trim/uppercase)
findings.whyItBreaks: normalizeFinding previously trimmed/uppercased raw.severity and defaulted unrecognized values to P1. The changed code accepts raw.severity only if it is exactly one of "P0".."P3" and otherwise falls back to P3. Any LLM/review output with lowercase ("p1"), surrounding whitespace (" P2 "), a typo, or a missing severity now silently becomes P3 (lowest) instead of P1 — a real defect classified as the mildest tier. The invalid-severity signal is downgraded rather than preserved, so consumers cannot distinguish a malformed finding from a legitimate low-severity one.

findings.title: GitHub tokens leak to spawned codex subprocess
findings.whyItBreaks: The base deliberately built `env = { ...process.env }` and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN, and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawning codex. The head removes that block and the `env:` option entirely, so spawnSync inherits the full parent environment. The codex CLI (an AI agent sandboxed to read-only, but still a subprocess that can read env vars and perform actions) now receives live GitHub credentials, exposing them to anything codex does with its environment. This is a direct regression of an intentional secret-hygiene control.

findings.title: GitHub tokens now leak to codex subprocess env
findings.whyItBreaks: The base version built an explicit env copy with GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN deleted before spawnSync. The change drops that block and the `env` option entirely; spawnSync with no `env` option inherits process.env verbatim, so the codex CLI (an external AI agent that can run shell commands) and any child process it spawns (e.g. `gh`, git, scripts) now see the parent's GitHub credentials. The `-s read-only` sandbox restricts filesystem writes but does not scrub environment variables or block network use, so the tokens are readable and usable by the subprocess. This was a deliberate security boundary and its removal is unexplained by the PR (prMeta is null; the diff is the only change).

findings.title: Codex subprocess now inherits GitHub tokens (env scrub removed)
findings.whyItBreaks: At base (29dd76d) runCodex explicitly copied process.env and deleted GH_TOKEN, GITHUB_TOKEN and GITHUB_API_TOKEN before spawnSync; the diff deletes those three lines plus the env construction, so the spawn now uses the default env, which is the full parent process environment. The spawned codex CLI (an LLM agent process, with cwd = opts.repoPath) now runs with GH_TOKEN/GITHUB_TOKEN/GITHUB_API_TOKEN present. Any code path (the agent itself, or a codex child process) that reads the environment, prints it, or is influenced by it can expose live GitHub credentials; at minimum the previously-enforced boundary between the controller process and the agent is gone. The scrub was part of the file's original design (added in the same base commit that introduced codex.ts), so this is a deliberate protection being removed, not an unused detail.

findings.title: Remove the fork-PR guard that protects the self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate preventing `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened) events from fork repos from running this job. After the deletion, a fork PR (head.repo.full_name != this repo) triggers the workflow, which then runs the fork's untrusted code on a self-hosted runner: `actions/checkout` with `ref: <head.sha>`, `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (executing the fork's install/lifecycle scripts from its package.json/lockfile), and `./node_modules/.bin/tsx src/cli.ts --github --pr ...`, all with `GH_TOKEN` set in env and `pull-requests: write` / `checks: write` permissions granted at workflow scope. This is the classic self-hosted-runner + fork-PR supply-chain hole; the base file was authored specifically with the guard (one-line deletion relative to base 08b6e15).

findings.title: Fork PRs now execute PR head on self-hosted runner
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted line `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only same-repo restriction on the job. Without it, `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened) fires for fork PRs, and the job checks out the PR head sha (ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha, line 23), runs `corepack enable && pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (line 28, which executes PR-controlled postinstall/build scripts), then runs `tsx src/cli.ts` — the PR's own code — on a self-hosted runner with the workflow-scoped GITHUB_TOKEN (line 33) and write permissions (pull-requests: write, checks: write, lines 13-14). A fork author gets arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted host and (for same-repo or once any secret is added) access to the token.

findings.title: Fork PRs now run untrusted code on self-hosted runner with token
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted `if: github.event.pull_request.head.repo.full_name == github.repository` was the only gate keeping fork PRs out. With it gone, any fork PR triggering `pull_request` (opened/synchronize/reopened) runs this job on the self-hosted runner: it checks out the fork's PR head (`ref: github.event.pull_request.head.sha`), runs `pnpm install --frozen-lockfile` (arbitrary install/postinstall scripts from the fork's package.json/lockfile), then executes the fork's `src/cli.ts` with `GH_TOKEN: secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN` and job permissions `pull-requests: write` and `checks: write`. A fork PR therefore gets arbitrary code execution on the self-hosted machine plus a write-scoped workflow token — the classic self-hosted-runner supply-chain bypass the guard existed to prevent.

findings.title: Explicit 0 duration env var silently discarded
findings.whyItBreaks: The predicate changed from `parsed >= 0` to `parsed > 0`, so an operator who sets NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (immediate SIGKILL after timeout) or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 (stop waiting for the escapee immediately) now silently receives 5000ms/2000ms instead. Both values feed setTimeout only (lines 123-124); grace=0 is a legitimate, previously-accepted config meaning 'no grace period'. The change silently substitutes a different behavior for an explicit operator setting with no log, doc, or error — the old `>= 0` clearly distinguished 0 as valid.

findings.title: readRunnerDurationMs: explicit 0 silently falls back to default
findings.whyItBreaks: Previously parsed >= 0 honored an explicit 0. After the change, NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 (valid, previously-working configs meaning 'no grace / no give-up') silently fall back to the hardcoded 5000ms (line 4-5) and 2000ms (line 7-8) defaults, with no log or error. The resulting RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS (used for the SIGTERM->SIGKILL timer at line 124) and RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS (used for the finish timer at line 123) can exceed the operator's configured value with no signal that the config was ignored, delaying the kill path.

findings.title: Explicit "0" env duration now silently discarded
findings.whyItBreaks: readRunnerDurationMs now rejects parsed === 0, so a caller that explicitly configures NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_TIMEOUT_GRACE_MS=0 (immediate SIGKILL after SIGTERM) or NEEDLEFISH_RUNNER_SIGKILL_GIVE_UP_MS=0 (finish immediately after hard kill, skip the close wait) is silently overridden with the 5000ms / 2000ms defaults. Previously those exact values were honored (>= 0). No doc/comment/commit justifies the narrower domain, and the two call sites (line 124 grace, line 123 give-up) read the result only as a setTimeout delay, so the change is observable in failure-path timing only.

findings.title: Coverage backstop removed: changed files can be silently never reviewed
findings.whyItBreaks: The deleted block computed `covered` from the selected hotspots and pushed a tail hotspot ("tail-coverage") for every changed file not in them, so no changed file was silently skipped. The only remaining guard is `slice(0, MAX_HOTSPOTS)` (line 93, MAX_HOTSPOTS=6), so any hotspot beyond the cap, or any changed file the map pass fails to assign to a hotspot, is never deep-reviewed and never appears in `checked` or in the output — the tool can report a clean review for a large PR while entirely missing files. This is a silent coverage drop in a review tool, not a cosmetic change.

findings.title: Deep-pass failure now aborts the entire large review
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch around the deep pass is deleted: `runCodex(deepPrompt, ...)` / `extractJson` / `normalizeReview` is now called bare, so any malformed/failed output from one hotspot throws out of reviewLarge, discarding every other hotspot's findings, the checked list, and the critic pass. Previously the catch recorded `[hotspot] DEEP PASS FAILED: ...` in `checked`, recorded a blocks:true residual risk, and continued with remaining hotspots — the review degraded instead of dying. The unhandled error also propagates to the caller instead of yielding a partial result with the failed hotspot clearly marked.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual_risks silently discarded; hardcoded empty array
findings.whyItBreaks: `candidateMerged.residual_risks` is now hardcoded to `[]` and the `residuals` array / `ResidualRisk` import are gone, so the deep passes' own residual_risks (the only place an honest 'this hotspot wasn't fully reviewed' signal existed) never reach the critic prompt or the final verdict. In the base, deep residuals were collected into candidateMerged.residual_risks and fed to the critic, which could propagate them into pruned.residual_risks (and thus deriveVerdict). Now the only residual signal is whatever the critic invents; a deep pass that reports unresolved residuals (or a failed deep pass marked blocks:true) produces no visible/blocking risk in the output.

findings.title: dedup key drops whyItBreaks; distinct findings over-merge
findings.whyItBreaks: The old key included `norm(f.whyItBreaks).slice(0, 80)`; the new key is only `file|lineStart|category|norm(title)` (title now sliced to 60 chars inside norm). Two findings at the same file/line/category whose titles share a 60-char prefix but genuinely describe different defects are now merged into one, and the lower-severity one is silently discarded (the loop keeps the higher SEV_RANK entry). This loses real findings, not just dedup bookkeeping. Note the slice(0,60) on the title alone (previously title was also slice(0,60)) is unchanged — the dropped whyItBreaks component is the behavior change.

findings.title: Coverage backstop removed — unselected files silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: hotspots are capped at MAX_HOTSPOTS (6) and files not mapped to any selected hotspot are now never deep-reviewed and never recorded. The removed code pushed a `tail-coverage` hotspot for exactly these files and its comment stated the invariant 'never silently skip a changed file'. With that gone, a bundle whose map pass returns >6 hotspots, or hotspots whose `files` omit some changed file, ends the review with those files completely unreviewed — no `checked` entry, no residual risk, no finding, and the critic is given a `summary` that presents the review as complete. This is the core guarantee of the large-PR path, not a cosmetic preference, and it silently degrades review coverage on precisely the large PRs this path exists for.

findings.title: Deep-pass failure no longer degrades — one failure aborts whole review
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch around the deep pass was removed and the `catch` arm (which recorded `checked.push('[name] DEEP PASS FAILED: ...')` and pushed a `blocks: true` residual, then continued the loop) is gone. Now any throw from `normalizeReview(extractJson(runCodex(...)))` — e.g. a malformed deep-pass response or a transient codex error — propagates out of reviewLarge, discarding all already-collected findings/checked from the successful hotspots, the map pass, and the critic/verdict entirely. The graceful-degradation contract (partial results + a blocking residual naming the unreviewed files) is gone; the failure is loud but leaves the review with zero usable output.

findings.title: Dedup key dropped whyItBreaks — distinct findings collapse
findings.whyItBreaks: The dedup key changed from `file|lineStart|category|norm(title)|norm(whyItBreaks)` to `file|lineStart|category|norm(title)` (the norm now also slices at 60, which matches the old `.slice(0, 60)` on the title — that part is equivalent). Two findings at the same file/lineStart/category with the same title but different whyItBreaks text now hash to one key; the higher-severity one wins and the other is silently dropped, losing its root-cause text and potentially a distinct defect. Dedup is designed to remove exact duplicates, not to merge distinct findings that share a title.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks silently discarded from critic input
findings.whyItBreaks: candidateMerged now hardcodes `residual_risks: []` (previously `residual_risks: residuals`, the aggregate of per-hotspot `res.residual_risks` plus the blocks:true failure residual). The critic is therefore never shown the caveats the deep passes reported and cannot retain/prune them; since final `residualRisks` come from the critic's output, every deep-pass residual risk is silently dropped on the large path. Successful deep passes now surface zero uncertainty to the critic or the final result.

findings.title: Remove tail-coverage backstop: files not mapped to a hotspot are silently skipped
findings.whyItBreaks: The map pass only assigns files to hotspots (and is capped at MAX_HOTSPOTS, line 93). The deleted block explicitly guaranteed that changed files not in any selected hotspot were still pushed into a tail hotspot ('never silently skip a changed file'). After this change, any file beyond the 6 hotspots or not assigned by the map (e.g. files the map pass missed) is never deep-reviewed, never appears in checked, and never appears in the result while the review reports success. Verified by comparing with git show HEAD~1:src/core/review.ts lines 97-107.

findings.title: Deep-pass failure now propagates and aborts the entire large review
findings.whyItBreaks: The try/catch around the deep pass was removed. runCodex/extractJson/normalizeReview can throw; previously that was caught, the failure was recorded in checked as 'DEEP PASS FAILED: ...' and a blocks:true residual risk was added (which the critic saw), and the loop continued with the remaining hotspots. Now the first deep-pass exception propagates out of reviewLarge and out of review(), discarding all findings/checked entries gathered for earlier hotspots and returning no result at all for the whole (large) PR. Verified against git show HEAD~1:src/core/review.ts.

findings.title: Dedup key dropped whyItBreaks; distinct findings collapse into one
findings.whyItBreaks: Old key was `${file}|${lineStart}|${category}|${norm(title).slice(0,60)}|${norm(whyItBreaks).slice(0,80)}`; new key is `${file}|${lineStart}|${category}|${norm(title)}` (norm now slices to 60). Two findings at the same file/line/category with the same title (or same 60-char title prefix) but different root causes/whyItBreaks now merge into one entry; the higher-severity one survives and the other is silently dropped from the output. A real finding (e.g. null deref vs race at the same line) is lost from the review result. Verified by comparing the norm/key lines against HEAD~1.

findings.title: Deep-pass residual risks discarded before they reach the critic
findings.whyItBreaks: The diff hardcoded candidateMerged.residual_risks to [] and removed residuals.push(...res.residual_risks) and the blocks:true residual for failed deep passes. In the base, per-hotspot residual risks (and the failure residual) were included in the candidate shown to the critic; now the critic always receives residual_risks: [], so blocked/incomplete coverage is invisible to the critic and can never influence the verdict or the returned summary. The success path also no longer carries the deep pass's own residuals anywhere.

findings.title: Focus/deep silently dropped from large-PR path
findings.whyItBreaks: reviewLarge previously forwarded bundle.focus and bundle.deep to the map prompt (mapBundle) and substituted {{FOCUS}} in deep.md. After this change the map pass no longer receives focus/deep, and the deep prompt chain no longer replaces {{FOCUS}}, so (a) user focus is silently ignored for large PRs and (b) if deep.md still contains the literal placeholder it is now sent verbatim to the model instead of the focus text. The small-PR path (reviewSmall, src/core/review.ts ~line 52) still forwards the whole bundle including focus/deep, so large vs small behavior is now inconsistent — focus handling diverges by path.

findings.title: Large-PR map pass drops focus and deep from mapBundle
findings.whyItBreaks: Base included `focus: bundle.focus, deep: bundle.deep` in mapBundle (base lines 90-91); the head omits them, so the map pass for a large PR no longer receives the user's focus steering or the deep flag. The small path (reviewSmall, lines 52-55) still JSON-stringifies the entire bundle including focus, so a user steering a large review toward specific files/areas loses that context only on the large path.

findings.title: Deep prompt no longer interpolates the focus placeholder
findings.whyItBreaks: The removed line `.replace("{{FOCUS}}", bundle.focus ?? "(none)")` means the deep prompt is built without focus: (a) if prompts/deep.md still contains {{FOCUS}}, the literal placeholder is sent to the model verbatim; (b) regardless of template, the user's focus never reaches the deep pass for a large PR, while the small path forwards the full bundle (including focus) via review.md.

findings.title: Seconds can round up to 60, producing 'Xm 60s'
findings.whyItBreaks: minutes = floor(ms/60000) and seconds = round((ms % 60000)/1000) are computed independently. For ms=119900: minutes=1, seconds=round(59900/1000)=60 → '1m 60s'. For ms=59999: minutes=0, seconds=round(59.999)=60 → '60s' (old code rendered '1m 0s'). The remainder never carries into minutes, so the displayed duration both exceeds the true total and is double-counted/inconsistent with the minutes shown. E.g. stats/total durations near a minute boundary (e.g. any call lasting ~60s) render as '60s' or 'Xm 60s'.

findings.title: formatDuration can print "60s" (e.g. "1m 60s")
findings.whyItBreaks: New code computes minutes = floor(ms/60000) and seconds = round((ms % 60000)/1000) separately. When the sub-minute remainder rounds up to 60, the output is invalid: ms = 119500 → \"1m 60s\" (old code rounded first then split, yielding \"2m 0s\"). ms = 59500 → \"60s\" (old: \"1m 0s\"). The caller (stats line in renderMarkdown, src/shared/render.ts:75) would render the misleading string.

findings.title: formatDuration can render "1m 60s" (seconds rounds to 60)
findings.whyItBreaks: The new code computes minutes from ms/60000 and then rounds only the sub-minute remainder. Whenever the remainder rounds up to 60 (e.g. ms=119_500 → minutes=1, seconds=Math.round(59.5)=60), the rendered string is "1m 60s", which is not a valid duration. Previously totalSeconds was rounded once and both minutes and the remainder were derived from it (totalSeconds=120 → "2m 0s"), which always produced a valid 0-59 second remainder. The same independent-rounding also produces "60s" (minutes=0) for ms=59_500 where the old code produced "1m 0s". Callers at src/shared/render.ts:75 and :80 feed arbitrary durationMs/totalDurationMs values into this function, so this malformed output lands in the user-facing markdown report.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger accepts 0 and blank input
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was relaxed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0`, so 0 now passes while the function name, error message ('requires a positive integer'), and prior behavior all promise >0. Worse, Number("") === 0 and Number("  ") === 0, so empty/whitespace input is silently accepted and returns 0 instead of throwing — a caller (e.g. a timeoutMs/retry-count option) gets 0 where a positive value was promised. No in-repo callers were found (rg over the repo), but this is an exported public helper, so the contract itself is the defect.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 and empty string as positive
findings.whyItBreaks: The check was changed from `parsed <= 0` to `parsed < 0` (line 32), so `parsePositiveInteger("0", "x")` now returns 0 instead of throwing, and `Number("") === 0` means an empty string also returns 0 silently. The exported name, the throw message (`${label} requires a positive integer`), and the function contract still promise a strictly positive integer, so every caller trusting the name/doc will receive 0 (or an empty-string coercion to 0) as a valid value. No in-repo callers exist to catch this, and the relaxed behavior is also a validation weakening on the only integer parser in the repo.

findings.title: parsePositiveInteger now accepts 0 but error/name promise positive
findings.whyItBreaks: The guard was changed from parsed <= 0 to parsed < 0, so Number('0') (and '0.0', '+0') now passes validation. The exported function is named parsePositiveInteger and its throw message still reads 'requires a positive integer', so any caller trusting the contract will treat 0 as valid when the stated contract excludes it. Downstream uses of the returned value (e.g. timeoutMs-style limits) cannot distinguish a legitimate 0 from the error path, and no in-repo caller enforces the promised positivity.
